items.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
items.content: At a glance Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model. Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable. AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error.  In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. Figure 1. Each finished session teaches TokenEconomizer something about the repository, so later sessions cost less tokens.   Where the tokens go We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s…

items.title: Import AI 481: AI sub-contractors; a wet lab for AI; and subterfuge during development
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better: …AI can now productively spend money to improve itself… Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks. 21 long-horizon tasks “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.” Example task: Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered. Key features: Scaling spending : “Give agents $10, $50, and $200 per task to spend on training compute and data, and evaluate whether agents can use the additional capital productively,” they write. “In our experiments, we find that stronger agents are able to reliably improve their submissions with greater access to capital.” Open-ended & end-to-end : “In each task, agents can choose architectures, source data, implement training, provision compute, evaluate checkpoints, and optimize inference,” they write. items.title: Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
items.content: Open video on YouTube ↗ Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Half the work on Linear is now created by agents Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs…
items.summary: >50% of tickets written by agents, the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR, and selling without SDRs or FDEs

items.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
items.content: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen , who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das , a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs . It inclu…

items.title: New Congress, New Rare Earths Policy?
items.content: Two announcements before we dive in: Remember when Jordan’s wife ran a ‘looking for a CTO’ post for an insuretech startup? Well, thanks to the ChinaTalk network, she found an incredible one . They’re now revenue positive and halfway through a seed round. Thank you all for the help! Jordan will be in DC the week after Thanksgiving for a hot minute and will be hosting a meetup on Dec 2nd. This piece was authored by anonymous contributor “Matteo Clavijero”. The blue wave of the midterms has put rare earth companies in the hot seat. Rare earths, particularly those used in the production of permanent magnets, are a critical input enabling trillions of dollars of downstream economic value. Beijing dominates the rare earth magnet supply chain from ore extraction to magnetization, with over 90% of mining, refining, and magnet-making concentrated in China. The CCP has repeatedly sought geopolitical leverage by exercising export restrictions on rare earths to constrict Western economies, and American rare earth competitors have been supported by industrial policy in response. After all, without rare earths the production of a laundry list of technologies — EVs, data centers, drones, wind turbines, smartphones, robots, and more — grinds to a halt. The US has been attempting to support an ex-China rare earth industry for the past decade, and government support is necessary for any ex-China industry to succeed. Projects are low-margin, decade-long investments that require the government to derisk and backstop ventures, such that the barriers to success are low enough that private investment takes the industry seriously. The second Trump administration has made a flurry of deals, replete with debt financing and equity purchases from the Export-Import Bank (EXIM) and the Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), ostensibly for the purpose of securing America’s critical mineral supply chains. But many deals h…

items.title: BIS Takes on Compute Leakage
items.content: A 132-page export control rule landed Monday morning, and the Commerce Department’s own press release credited Treasury and the NSC with writing it. Days after the Megaspeed scandal ended Jensen Huang’s run at Nvidia, Washington is moving to close the cloud loophole that, by ChinaTalk’s estimate, supplies two-fifths of China’s AI compute. Two Biden NSC alumni weigh in: ⁠Chris McGuire⁠ , now senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations after a stint as deputy senior director for technology and national security, and ⁠Julian Gewirtz⁠ , the former senior director for China and Taiwan affairs now a senior research scholar at Columbia SIPA. We discuss… Three loopholes closed in 132 pages — license requirements for chips headed to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil; a cap on compute rented to Chinese firms; and a TSMC backdoor closed for the second time. The Northern Virginia problem — why a rule that stops at the US border could simply move China’s rented compute from Johor to the Washington suburbs. Who wrote the rule — what crediting Treasury and the NSC says about Commerce’s credibility, and whether Trump holds firm in Shenzhen. Does Xi know the numbers — whether Beijing escalates or doubles down on the bet that it can (again) talk Trump into loosening controls. Jensen’s soup vendor — the customer-concentration fear that pushed Nvidia toward Asian neoclouds and China. Zero consequences for three million chips — why export controls need their BNP Paribas moment, and what that has to do with AI safety. Listen now on your favorite podcast platform . items.title: MOFCOM's New Rules: Digging For Leverage
items.content: With the world scrambling to diffuse China’s rare earth weapon, Chinese regulators have apparently been tasked with identifying alternative sources of potential leverage. MOFCOM’s recent work created legal mechanisms to restrict the flow of a curious collection of products: tunnel boring machines, dredging components, solar manufacturing equipment, biotechnology, and drones. At first glance, this seems like an eclectic list, but these technologies are connected beyond the fact that they are all made in China. Today, we’re unpacking the geopolitical incentives that made them MOFCOM’s business. This is part two of our series on MOFCOM’s October 2026 regulatory drops. In part one, we analyzed the October 16th proposals for regulating AI technologies. Today’s installment tackles the October 16th proposals for biotech and solar and the mixed bag from October 19th. We explore: Why parsing China’s trade policy requires looking beyond the US-China rivalry to Beijing’s bilateral relations with other capitals — and why India in particular is under fire; How tunnel boring machines and dredgers help us understand China’s ambitions as a regional power; Beijing’s playbook for keeping foreign countries dependent on its solar provisions; And, what biotech and drones tell us about China’s approach to intellectual property. ChinaTalk is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. items.title: Jensen Out, MATCH Act In?
items.content: Jordan Schneider, Dylan Patel, and Jordan Nanos of SemiAnalysis record an emergency pod after Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO. We discuss: Why Jensen’s exit could become cover for “really stupid laws” — and why Dylan backs the MATCH Act but thinks RASA is a mistake. The game theory of remote access: renting compute to Chinese firms as margin capture and a kill switch, versus closing the Malaysia loophole outright. “Flip the table”: why equipment controls beat chip and model controls, and how close Huawei’s silicon now is. Why no American lab has out-built Kimi or DeepSeek in open models. Nvidia without Jensen: talent retention, Rubin and Feynman execution risk, and who should run the company. Colette Kress’s exposure, Supermicro and Megaspeed, and a fight over whether this amounts to the “nationalization” of Nvidia. Listen now on your favorite podcast app . Jensen Resigns Jordan Nanos: Hey, Dylan. Hey, Jordan. Did you guys hear the CEO of the world’s largest and most important company just resigned? Dylan Patel: No. Jordan Nanos: Are you serious? What could possibly have led to that? Well, there are allegations of some pretty serious conduct violations. Apparently you can’t sleep with your subordinates and keep your job. Readers vote on next week’s feature translation by replying to the email and/or commenting on the post with the number of your preferred article. *Extra weight goes to votes from those of you who support ChinAI through a paid subscription.
